match.reason: No point in the bank teaches cash flow management strategies; the closest one only names cash flow problems as a cause of small business failure, which is a different and broader idea.

draft.title: Cash flow management
card: Cash flow is the money moving in and out of a business. A business can be profitable and still run short of cash when bills fall due before customers pay.
Spread payments
timing big outlays, such as insurance, rent or tax, across the year in smaller amounts, so no single month drains the bank account.
Discounts
offering customers a lower price if they pay early, such as 2% off if paid within 7 days. The business gets cash sooner but receives slightly less per sale.
Factoring
selling unpaid invoices to a finance company for immediate cash, less a fee. The business gets most of the money now instead of waiting for customers.
draft.remember: Cash flow strategies bring cash in sooner or push payments out in smaller amounts, so bills can be paid on time.

a.q: Why might a profitable business still need cash flow management?
opts: Bills may fall due before customers pay their invoices
Profit is only counted once all the stock is sold
Profit cannot be used to pay for wages and rent
Profit shows the cash in the bank on a given day
a.why: Profit and cash are different. A business can make sales at a profit but wait weeks for payment, while wages and rent are due now. The option saying profit shows the bank balance is wrong because sales on credit raise profit before any cash arrives.
a.clue: Think about when money is earned and when it is received.

b.q: Priya's printing firm in Geelong has many unpaid customer invoices and a large wage bill due this week. Which action gives her cash fastest?
opts: Factor the unpaid invoices to a finance company
Offer new customers a discount for paying early
Spread next year's insurance across monthly payments
Wait for customers to pay within their usual terms
b.why: Factoring turns invoices already issued into cash straight away, less a fee. An early payment discount only helps with future sales and customers may still pay late. Spreading insurance eases later outlays but does not bring in cash for this week's wages.
b.clue: Which option works on invoices that already exist?

a.best: Bills may fall due before customers pay their invoices

b.best: Factor the unpaid invoices to a finance company

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a softening qualifier ('may') and the only one not starting with 'Profit'. The wrong options are absolute ('cannot', 'only'), so a test-wise student could pick it without knowing the idea.

card: Cash flow is the money moving in and out of a business. Profit counts a sale when it is made, even if the customer pays later, so a profitable business can still run short of cash when bills fall due first.
Spread payments

proposal.remember: Cash flow strategies bring cash in sooner or push payments out in smaller amounts, so bills can be paid on time.

a.q: Why can a profitable business still run short of cash?
opts: Credit sales count as profit before the cash comes in
Cash comes in before the sale is counted as profit
Profit is counted when stock is bought, not when sold
Profit is the same as the cash held in the bank
a.why: Profit counts a sale when it is made, but a customer buying on credit may pay weeks later, while wages and rent are due now. The option saying cash comes in first reverses this: with credit sales, the profit is recorded before the cash arrives.
a.clue: Think about when a sale is counted and when it is paid for.
